04 · Read & review

The transcript

Submit all six answers to unlock the transcript. You can then listen and read together.

The latest attachment from Fiona Bell was reassuring in exactly the way Emma had learnt to distrust. It was a clean, carefully formatted model decision notice for the Glenarraidh Education Trust's 2011 student travel programme. Blank fields invited an applicant's name, course and decision date. Beneath the proposed outcome, a paragraph advised rejected candidates that they could request reconsideration in writing within fourteen days.

Its language was consistent with the procedural guidance Fiona had sent the previous day. That consistency mattered: the two documents described the same intended mechanism. Yet Emma refused to mistake a coherent paper system for a verified history of its operation.

“A standard letter is evidence that notification was planned,” she told Sarah. “It doesn't establish that notices were issued, delivered or understood.”

Fiona had released the template because it contained no identifying information. She had not found a completed copy, and the folder marked Appeals and reviews remained unopened. Nor had she identified the person responsible for independently reviewing unsuccessful decisions. None of those gaps demonstrated misconduct. They indicated the limits of what the accessible material could substantiate.

Emma reread the contemporary parent's complaint in the local newspaper. Its author had criticised the opacity of the student selection process but had made no claim about the receipt of a formal decision notice. The omission could mean several things, including a simple choice to focus the published letter on another grievance. Inferring that the parent was never notified would be speculation.

A reply from the newspaper's archive complicated matters further. Staff believed that some unpublished correspondence from 2011 might survive, but they had not inventoried the relevant boxes. Access to any personal letters would require a separate assessment. Emma had neither a new witness nor a corroborated account; merely another possible archive to approach responsibly.

Back at the template, a seemingly routine instruction attracted her attention: Copy to scheme administrator. It suggested that the trust had contemplated keeping an internal duplicate. It did not specify who held that office or whether copies had been retained in practice.

Emma drafted a request that deliberately excluded personal details. Was there a register showing how many decision notices were issued, when they were sent and whether copies were routinely filed? She asked for the existence and format of records before requesting access to any of their contents.

Sarah suggested describing the scheme as one in which applicants had been guaranteed a route of appeal. Emma revised the sentence. The documentation provided for a review route; it did not show that the route was communicated to every eligible person, much less that any review had taken place.

The old newspaper's disputed figure of eight selected students remained unresolved. So did the separate questions of applicants, selections and payments. A dispatch register, if one existed, might help establish a decision count, but Emma would still need to distinguish a letter prepared from one actually sent, and a letter sent from one received.

She added those distinctions to her notebook. The deeper the investigation went, the less useful it became to ask what the trust had meant to do. The more precise question was what contemporary records could demonstrate that it had done.
